claims.text: Controlled thermal oxidation of Q235 steel can produce an adherent surface oxide film.
The thermally formed film on Q235 steel is primarily Fe3O4 or Fe2O3.
The preformed oxide film inhibits ingress of corrosive species at room temperature.
Elevated temperature may degrade the oxide film and promote localized corrosion.
The initial material is as-received Q235 carbon steel with its native microstructure and composition.
Dry-air oxidation at 150–300 °C for varying durations can be used to engineer the surface oxide characteristics.
The oxide layer's nature, thickness, and adhesion govern its effectiveness as a barrier against corrosive species.
An adherent oxide film limits diffusion of chloride ions, oxygen, and water to the underlying Q235 steel.
The preformed oxide film remains coherent and protective at room temperature.
Thermal expansion and stress at 70–100 °C can cause spallation or microcracking of the oxide film.
Spallation or microcracking compromises the film and accelerates localized corrosion.
Optimally pre-oxidized Q235 samples will have lower corrosion rates than untreated Q235 under both room-temperature and elevated-temperature exposure.
Reduced weight loss and higher electrochemical impedance will indicate lower corrosion rates.
Treated and untreated Q235 specimens will be compared in 3.5 wt.% NaCl at room temperature and 70–100 °C under controlled oxygen and humidity.
Oxidation behavior may differ outside the fixed chloride, humidity, oxygen, and temperature ranges used in the study.
The threshold temperature for oxide-film degradation and the long-term kinetics of spallation are uncertain.
The experiment includes an untreated Q235 control exposed under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed measurements are weight loss, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and SEM assessment of film morphology and spallation.

contradictions.description: The predicted-outcome field says decisive falsification requires similar or higher corrosion under both temperature regimes, whereas the detailed falsification rule permits falsification based on failure at room temperature alone or on absence of elevated-temperature film degradation.

Elevated-temperature film degradation is described as conditional and its onset threshold as uncertain, yet failure to observe degradation within 70–100 °C is treated as falsifying the whole hypothesis.
